            b*esp.Br + b*esp.Ar
oc.Ar ~     lstm +  lstsd + evim + evisd + dem + wdist + mrvbf + vdchn + twi +
            a*esp.Br + a*esp.Ar + btr + thick.Ar
esp.Ar ~    lstm +  lstsd + dem + wdist + mrvbf + vdchn + twi + river + evisd +
            esp.Br
esp.Br ~    lstm +  lstsd + dem + wdist + mrvbf + vdchn + twi + river + evisd

sat.A ~~    0.20*sat.A

Modification Indices:

  arguments imply differing number of rows: 177, 175

If I not constrain the coefficients, the function works well. Same happens with package semPlot:

Error in data.frame(label = pars$label, lhs = ifelse(pars$op == "~" |  :

  arguments imply differing number of rows: 173, 1, 175

Any suggestion?

Thanks,
Marcos

> > I have tried to estimate this model in two ways:
> >
> > a) Use X1 as a grouping factor. This is problematic though, because it doesn't really let me give a good estimator of the marginal effect of moving between the two groups moderated by M
>
>
> Wouldn't the marginal effect of M on Y be estimated by a model with equality constraints on the effect of M on Y across groups (X1)?
>
> Y ~ c(b, b)*M
>
> That model would be nested within the model without the equality constraint, and the chi-squared difference test would be a test of the H0 that interaction == 0.  Assuming you have large enough sample sizes in each group, another advantage of the multiple-groups approach would be that the marginal effect of M on Y from the constrained model could be estimated without assuming homogeneity of error variances across groups, which the use of a dummy variable would have to assume.
>
> Terry

messages.body_plain:
> I tried to use semTools::reliability() with a CFA  that has some single-indicator-latents and i get this error:
> "Error in trueitem + erritem : non-conformable arrays"
>
> What does this mean? Is this because you can´t get reliability values for the si-latents? Is there a workaround?

Programmatically, there is probably an issue with single-indicator constructs such that a matrix might reduce to a vector unless "drop = FALSE" is specified in brackets.  Conceptually, there is no way to estimate reliability of a test with only one item.  The formula for alpha would end up dividing by zero in the k / (k - 1) term.  The formula for AVE or omega should work out to 1 because the error variance is fixed to zero (unless you fix it to another quantity based on reliability, in which case your reliability estimate would be the same as the one you already have), so the numerator and denominator are the same quantity.

My suggestion is to just take out the single-indicator constructs and calculate reliability among the rest.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
So are HIS1, HIS2, HIS3, HIS4 your four occasions? If they are, and each individual is just one line of the data, then you don't have anything to cluster for. If you had scales administered four times, and you wanted to build a model where the latent construct is your latent variable, and items are the observed variables, then the idea of clustering could have been entertained to model the dependencies between the four occasions over time. As it stands, however, you have a CFA with no structure imposed; a very reasonable question to ask is whether you have measurement invariance between the occasions -- but it looks like motivation and emotion will likely fail that due to something odd happening on the third occasion.

messages.body_plain:
Oh I see. Well your models aren't exactly the same with and without clustering. With clustering, the standard errors are different (as they should be; the point estimates should be the same). Also, with clustering, you should forget about the MLM fit test statistic reported (the 212 number), and only look at the "robust" statistic reported (the 138 number).

On Thu, Nov 5, 2015 at 3:12 PM, Aaron Charlton <aaronbc...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi, Stas.
> Not exactly. HIS1-HIS4 are four different scale items that hopefully measure the latent variable 'history'. My occasions are contained in the 'stimulus' variable, a factor with four levels. I have the data in long form, so there are 4 observations for each person (ID) -- one for each of the four stimuli. Thanks. -Aaron
>
> On Thursday, November 5, 2015 at 12:44:35 PM UTC-8, Stas Kolenikov wrote:
> > So are HIS1, HIS2, HIS3, HIS4 your four occasions? If they are, and each individual is just one line of the data, then you don't have anything to cluster for. If you had scales administered four times, and you wanted to build a model where the latent construct is your latent variable, and items are the observed variables, then the idea of clustering could have been entertained to model the dependencies between the four occasions over time. As it stands, however, you have a CFA with no structure imposed; a very reasonable question to ask is whether you have measurement invariance between the occasions -- but it looks like motivation and emotion will likely fail that due to something odd happening on the third occasion.

> Besides prediction, I also want to test is there any causal-effects within the variables and with the outcome (subspecises), i.e., which variables contribute/decide to the differences among them. I think SEM could be a way for this aim, but just don't know how to organize the analysis.

It sounds like you might consider your plant characteristics as indicators of subspecies, which could be considered a categorical latent variable.  Look into latent class analysis and latent profile analysis, which unfortunately will not be available in lavaan for some time.  the R package "nlsem" can fit finite mixture models, but if you are a novice in SEM, using that package might be an uphill battle (but worth the effort, if that is what you want to do).  In Mplus, you could fit 2 latent class models: one with known classes (since it seems you already have that variable recorded) and one with unknown classes, to see how closely the results align with your known classes.  There might be some other validation methods I'm unaware of -- I am not experienced with latent class models.  If you can't locate any satisfactory literature on fitting latent class models, you could post your question on SEMNET for help.  If you have an Mplus license, their forum could also provide help fitting your model (again, if that is indeed the type of model you want to fit).

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Dear Lavaan Group,
   I am a graduate student, new to Lavaan, and really appreciate any help.  I am hoping to determine if variable A (continuous variable) affects variable D (a binary, factor variable) either directly or indirectly through variable B (a continuous variable) or variable C (a binary, factor variable).  One problem I have is  that the relationship is quadratic between A and D and also between B and D (all other relationships are linear).  I am a little confused on how to include these quadratic variables in Lavaan.    I am hoping to compare these three pathways (one direct and two indirect) with AIC.  I have seen the postings for determining one indirect pathway but am unsure of how to compare two indirect pathways (with each other and also with the direct pathway).  I've attached part of my data and the model I am hoping to examine.  I've included my coding attempts below although I have been unable to correct the error message it is giving for looking at indirect/direct effects (error: "missing observed variables in dataset").  I may be missing something, but as far as I understand, I have defined these variables in my model.  Thank you for any feedback/ideas,
Ellen

data=read.csv("Ellen_data.csv")

data$Aquad=data$A^2  #get quadratic of A
data$Bquad=(data$B^2)/100  #Get quadratic of B.
                                                #I divided by 100 to make the variance more comparable with other variables
#the overall model
model='D~A+Aquad+B+Bquad+C
             B~A
             C~A'
fit=sem(model,data=data,fixed.x=F)
summary(fit)

#get direct/indirect/total effects
model_all='D~A*a+Aquad*d+B*b+Bquad*d+C*c
             B~A*f
             C~A*g
            direct:=a*d
            indirect1:=f*b*d
            indirect2:=g*c
            total:= (a*d)+(f*b*d)+(g*c)'
fit_all=sem(model_all,data=data,fixed.x=F)
summary(fit_all)
AICc(fit_all)

#first indirect pathway
model_indirect1='C~A*g
             D~A*a+Aquad*d+C*c
            indirect:=g*c
            direct:=a*d
            total:=(g*c)+(a*d)'
fit_indirect1=sem(model_indirect1,data=data,fixed.x=F)
summary(fit_indirect1)
AICc(fit_indirect1)

#second indirect pathway
model_indirect2='B~A*f
             D~A*a+Aquad*d+B*b+Bquad*d
            indirect:=f*b*d
            direct:=a*d
            total:=(f*b*d)+(a*d)'
fit_indirect2=sem(model_indirect2,data=data,fixed.x=F)
summary(fit_indirect2)
AICc(fit_indirect2)

#direct pathway only
model_direct='D~A+Aquad'
fit_direct=sem(model_direct,data=data,fixed.x=F)
summary(fit_direct)
AICc(fit_direct)

#compare the three pathways
model.sel(fit_indirect1,fit_indirect2,fit_direct)

AIC is for comparing models (with the same data, but not the same parameters, or even the same parameterization), not for comparing parameter estimates.

You already defined parameters indirect1 and indirect2.  If you want to test whether their difference is zero (i.e., the null hypothesis  that they are the same), you can define a parameter for their difference as well.  For example:

> indirectDiff := indirect1 - indirect2

>             indirect2:=g*c
>             total:= (a*d)+(f*b*d)+(g*c)'

You need to put the labels before the variable names, not after.  lavaan interprets 'D~A*a' as the effect of variable a on variable D (labeled A), not the effect of A on D (labeled a).

messages.body_plain:
When you convert the variables in your data.frame to ordered factors, then the "ordered" argument in the lavaan/cfa/sem function is redundant.  Given that you have so many categorical indicators (all with 5 categories), you should expect estimation problems.  I can see you set the max number of iterations to 1000 -- why?  Could you even get your model to converge on a solution?  I couldn't.

You might want to read this study about treating ordinal variables as continuous:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0029315

I would advise you to do so, because your model is too big and your sample is too small to expect it to work, even if your complex model were correctly specified.  Judging from the results when treating the indicators as continuous, I expect you have gross misspecification to investigate before you could trust factor scores (which are already indeterminate, a problem exacerbated by having fewer indicators -- 3 of your 2nd-order factors have only 2 first-order "indicators").  And several model-implied factor correlations exceed 1, suggesting you should start with the first-order factor model to identify any divergent validity problems among those 8 factors, before positing that they measure 4 more higher-order factors.

Anyway, disregarding the problems with your model, I had no problem extracting factor scores from the model that actually converged.  See syntax below.

messages.body_plain:
Might have something to do with the fact that Z is highly correlated with the covariate that explains missingness.  And you are imposing missingness on all variables (Y, X, Z) using the same mechanism, so most of the time one variable is missing, the whole row is missing.  So among the complete rows, the same regression model still holds, and the only thing that should change is your power (I think).  But you are right -- the effects of missing mechanisms are more complicated than just MCAR / MAR.  Sophia Rabe-Hasketh showed some odd situations in a 2014 presentation you can access here:

http://www.modeling.uconn.edu/m3c/assets/File/Rabe-Hesketh.pdf

You might find some clues in there, or at least references for further reading.  But doing simulations like you are doing might be the fastest way to learn about any particular scenario you are worried about in a real-data situation.

By the way, you seem to redundantly generate Y from the regression model as well as using mvrnorm(), where in S it is uncorrelated with anything else.  Perhaps you mean to generate the uncorrelated errors "e" as the 4th row/column in S, instead of generating e independently in a call to univariate rnorm().  Including e in S (and then constructing Y in your regression model) would enable you to see the effect of having the covariate correlate with the errors, which I assume  would introduce bias in point estimates and Type I error rates.

Also, you might find the last example on the ?impose help page useful.  It demonstrates how to use a logistic regression formula to apply MAR, where the intercept is the overall proportion missing you want, and the slopes indicate the effect of the covariate (on whichever particular variable(s) you want to have missingness).

Terry

The error occurs on line 753 of the source code sim.R, in a hidden function called runRep(), which runs a single replication within the sim() function.

> implied <- fitted(attr(data, "fit"))

The problem occurs when trying to extract model-implied moments from a lavaan object which has not actually been fitted.  In this case, the fitted() method returns the error you see, but using lavInspect(fit, "cov.ov") and lavInspect(fit, "mean.ov") would return the needed information, although in a different format.  I'm not sure if the fitted() method used to work and something recently changed in lavaan, but I submitted a bug report on simsem's github site, with a link to this thread.

Until it gets fixed, I think you can get around the problem by using LISREL matrices (which I think is a safer method anyway) instead of lavaan syntax to specify your models.  See the first example on the ?model help page for syntax that is similar to your lavaan syntax.

> loading <- matrix(0, 6, 2)
> loading[1:3, 1] <- NA
> loading[4:6, 2] <- NA
> LY <- bind(loading, 0.7)
>
> latent.cor <- matrix(NA, 2, 2)
> diag(latent.cor) <- 1
> RPS <- binds(latent.cor, 0.5)
>
> TE <- binds(diag(NA, nrow = 6), diag(.51, nrow = 6))
>
> CFA.Model <- model(LY = LY, RPS = RPS, TE = TE, modelType = "CFA")
>
> dist2 <- bindDist(skewness = seq(-3, 3, length.out=6), kurtosis = seq(2, 5, length.out=6))
> summary(dist2)
>
> Output <- sim(5, model=CFA.Model, n=150, indDist = dist2)

This works.  Granted, this example assumes the population and analysis models are the same, like in your example.  But it also works if you have a different analysis model (e.g., a 1-factor model):

> LY.an <- bind(matrix(NA, 6, 1), 0.7)
> PS.an <- binds(matrix(1, 1, 1), 1)
> analysisModel <- model(LY = LY.an, PS = PS.an, TE = TE, modelType = "CFA")
> Output2 <- sim(5, model = analysisModel, generate=CFA.Model, n=150, indDist = dist2)

Hope this is sufficient to keep your study going.  Good luck!

Terry

messages.subject_clean: Dealing with endogeneity in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues:

Consider the population model below, and the data that is created based on it with the function simulateData( ). Note that, due to the design of the population model, the latent variable CO is correlated with SU's residual, which leads to the issue of endogeneity.

mPopModel <- '
# outer model
DM =~ DM1
CO =~ CO1
GT =~ 0.6*GT1 + 0.6*GT2 + 0.7*GT3 + 0.7*GT4 + 0.8*GT5
AC =~ 0.5*AC1 + 0.6*AC2 + 0.6*AC3 + 0.7*AC4 + 0.7*AC5
SU =~ 0.55*SU1 + 0.6*SU2 + 0.65*SU3 + 0.7*SU4 + 0.75*SU5
# inner model
DM ~ 0.0*CO
GT ~ 0.516*CO
AC ~ 0.288*CO
SU ~ 0.029*CO + 0.0*DM + 0.575*GT + 0.338*AC
'
mData_NORM <- simulateData(mPopModel,sample.nobs=10000L,std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE,standardized=TRUE)

Apparently running the SEM analysis below leads to incorrect estimations for the regressions, particularly for the following two regressions: GT ~ CO and AC ~ CO.

mModel <- '
# outer model
DM =~ DM1
CO =~ CO1
GT =~ GT1 + GT2 + GT3 + GT4 + GT5
AC =~ AC1 + AC2 + AC3 + AC4 + AC5
SU =~ SU1 + SU2 + SU3 + SU4 + SU5
# inner model
DM ~ CO
GT ~ CO
AC ~ CO
SU ~ CO + DM + GT + AC
'
mFit_NORM <- sem(mModel,data=mData_NORM)
summary(mFit_NORM)

Running the analysis in two stages seems to solve the problem. That is, first including only DM ~ CO, GT ~ CO, and AC ~ CO; and then only SU ~ CO + DM + GT + AC.

However, I was wondering if there is a setting in lavaan that solves the problem, without my having to conduct a two-stage analysis.

Can anyone help?

Ned Kock

PS: If I use the Factor-Based PLS Type CFM1 algorithm in WarpPLS, the regressions (and other parameters) are correctly estimated in one single run, without the need for a two-stage analysis. This occurs in spite of endogeneity, which is clearly visible in the data.

messages.subject_clean: effect coding and "measurement error accounted for"
messages.body_plain:
> how can I set my model but using the "effect coding" for scaling in lavaan?

By using labels for model parameters and setting nonlinear parameter constraints.  For example, in a 3-indicator factor:

> f =~ L1*x1 + L2*x2 + L3*x3
> x1 ~ T1*1
> x2 ~ T2*1
> x3 ~ T3*1
> ## parameter constraints
> L3 == 3 - L1 - L2
> T3 == 0 - T1 - T2

> A conceptual question. It is said that the Latent approach account for the "measurement error" in the measures, but how that happens from an algorithmic or mathematical perspective?

The short answer is that measurement error is explicitly represented as parameters in the model.  Point estimates of factor loadings and residual (measurement error) variances are chosen that best reproduce the observed covariance matrix.  There are many SEM textbooks available that describe the details of how measurement-model parameters are identified and estimated, using any number of algorithms (e.g., maximum likelihood).  This sort of general SEM question is better posted on the SEMNET forum:

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

Terry

But I don't imagine the bias is big relative to the size of MI you might consider noteworthy, nor that the EPCs are would be noticeably biased.
